title: The Sun’s outer atmosphere is 200 times hotter than its surface
body: The Sun’s visible surface, the photosphere, is about 5,800 K. Move outward into the faint corona, the halo seen during a total eclipse, and the temperature climbs to **1 to 2 million kelvin**. That is backwards from everyday experience, where things cool as you move away from the heat source, and it has been an unsolved problem for decades. The clue came from a mystery green line in the corona’s light, once blamed on an unknown element nicknamed ‘coronium’. In 1940, following Walter Grotrian’s work, Bengt Edlén showed it comes from iron atoms stripped of many of their electrons, something only extreme heat can do.

slides.label: the typical temperature of the Sun’s corona
slides.text: The visible surface below it is only about 5,800 K.

left.label: Expect
left.text: Like a campfire, the Sun should get cooler the farther you move from its core.

right.label: Observed
right.text: The temperature drops through the photosphere, then soars by a factor of about 200 in the thin corona above it.

slides.heading: Suspects for the heating
items: Waves: energy carried up along magnetic fields, an idea from Evry Schatzman in 1949
Reconnection: snapping magnetic field lines drive electric currents in the corona
Nanoflares: countless tiny flares, proposed by Eugene Parker

slides.question: What revealed that the corona is incredibly hot?
options: A green line from stripped iron atoms
slides.explanation: The mystery line once blamed on ‘coronium’ comes from iron atoms missing many electrons, which happens only at around a million degrees. Edlén showed this in 1940.
